newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU challenges U.S. origin rules on textiles.
newsitem.headline: EU challenges U.S. origin rules on textiles.

text.p: The European Commission challenged on Thursday recent U.S. laws on clothes' labelling, saying they could cost European manufacturers millions of dollars in lost sales.
Under the rules, the United States requires that clothes be labelled according to the country of origin of their raw material rather than the country where they were produced.
According to the rules, adopted in July this year, a silk tie designed, printed and made in Italy would have to bear a "Made in China" label in U.S. stores if the raw silk originated in China.

The Commission's challenge follows a complaint by the Italian Textile Federation, Federtessile, that the rules denied their products the "Made in Italy" label, meaning the Italian quality label was lost as a selling point for U.S. customers.
The Commission said the rules contravened U.S. commitments under two World Trade Organisation (WTO) agreements; on textiles and clothing and on rules of origin.

The Commission also accused Washington of denying the free market access guaranteed to the European Union in the Uruguay Round trade talks since the clothes were no longer considered as originating in the EU and were thus subject to import quotas.

The Commission said its complaint was a first step under the EU's so-called Trade Barriers Regulation that allows individual companies as well as industry groups and countries to ask the Commission to act against specific trade barriers.
Other steps could involve turning to WTO dispute settlement procedures or adopting retaliatory measures as authorised by the relevant dispute settlement body.
